title: Data, tables and graphs
soi: Data displays and summaries make patterns visible, but choices of grouping, scale and denominator shape the claims that seem reasonable.
engage: How can the same survey support a fair decision without letting a misleading graph or an unstated denominator do the arguing?
atl: In order for a student to process and communicate information, students must organise data, choose an appropriate representation, calculate summaries and justify a claim with its limitations.
objectives: Classify variables and organise frequency or two-way tables.
Construct and interpret bar and pie charts.
Summarise distributions with dot plots, histograms and averages.
Describe trends and detect misleading scales or claims.
vocabulary: variable · categorical · nominal · ordinal · discrete · continuous · frequency · two-way table · bar chart · pie chart · sector angle · dot plot · histogram · mean · median · mode · range · outlier · trend

sections.title: Data, variables and tables
sections.intent: Identify what was measured, the unit, the population and the type of variable before summarising.
paras: Data are recorded values. A categorical variable names groups (nominal) or ordered categories (ordinal). A numerical variable is discrete if it counts separate values, or continuous if it measures on a scale.
A frequency table lists categories or intervals and their counts. Frequencies must sum to the number of observations. A two-way table shows how two categories overlap.

example.title: Classify variables
example.problem: Lunch choice, year group, number of siblings and height.
steps: Year group: ordinal categorical (or discrete numerical code).
Siblings: discrete numerical. Height: continuous numerical.
example.answer: The variable type guides the display and summary.

sections.warning: A number used as a label (such as a shirt size code) is not automatically a quantity to average.

practice.prompt: Classify: favourite fruit, school year, number of pets, height.
practice.answer: Nominal categorical; ordinal categorical; discrete numerical; continuous numerical.
practice.reasoning: Name, order, count and measurement are different variable types.

practice.prompt: A table has frequencies 38, 31, 27 for school lunch in Years 7–9. Find the total.
Why is “year group” not usually averaged as if it were height?
practice.answer: It is an ordered category or label; an average year code may not describe a meaningful category.

practice.prompt: In a two-way table, Year 7 has 38 school, 24 packed, 8 off-site. Find the row total and the school-lunch share of Year 7.
practice.reasoning: Row total 70; use the row as denominator.

practice.prompt: A survey records “0, 1, 2, 3” as codes for four lunch choices. Can these codes be added meaningfully?
practice.answer: No. They are category labels, not counts or measurements.
practice.reasoning: Nominal codes have no numerical order or distance.

practice.prompt: A frequency table has total 200 and known frequencies 96 and 74. Find the missing frequency and its percentage.

diagram.caption: A frequency table organises categories; the counts sum to the 200 students surveyed.

sections.title: Bar charts and pie charts
sections.intent: Use bars to compare categories and sectors to show parts of one whole.
paras: A bar chart uses equal-width bars with heights proportional to frequency. Label axes, start the frequency axis at zero and keep spacing consistent.
A pie chart represents a whole by 360°. Sector angle = category frequency/total × 360°. Percentages should sum to 100% apart from stated rounding.
sections.warning: A pie chart is poor for comparing many similar categories or several groups side by side; a clustered bar chart is clearer.

practice.prompt: Find pie-chart angles for frequencies 96, 74 and 30 out of 200.
What percentage of 200 is 96?
Why should a bar-chart frequency axis start at zero?
practice.answer: Bar height encodes frequency; a truncated axis exaggerates differences.
practice.reasoning: Start the frequency axis at zero so the visual ratio matches the data ratio.

practice.prompt: Year 7 has 70 students, Year 8 and Year 9 have 65 each. Which display compares lunch choices across years?
practice.answer: A clustered bar chart (or a well-labelled two-way table).
practice.reasoning: It keeps year groups visible side by side.

practice.prompt: Three sector percentages are 48%, 37% and 15%. Do they fit one whole?
practice.reasoning: A pie chart partitions the whole.

practice.prompt: A category has sector angle 54° in a survey of 200. Find its frequency.

diagram.caption: Sector angles are proportional to frequency: 172.8°, 133.2° and 54°.

sections.title: Dot plots, histograms and averages
sections.intent: Describe shape, centre and spread; choose an average that fits the data and the question.
paras: A dot plot shows individual values. A histogram groups continuous or finely measured numerical data into intervals; with equal widths, bar height is frequency. State the boundary rule.
Mean = sum÷count; median is the middle ordered value (or mean of the two middle values); mode is most frequent; range = maximum−minimum. Outliers pull the mean more than the median.

example.title: Summarise 30 screen-time values
example.problem: The ordered data have sum 4,740; the 15th and 16th values are 135 and 140; 120 occurs four times.

sections.warning: For grouped data, a midpoint estimate of the mean is an estimate, not the exact mean of the raw values.

practice.prompt: Find the mean, median, mode and range of 2, 3, 3, 8.
For the 30 screen-time values, sum 4,740, middle values 135 and 140, mode 120, min 45, max 360. Find all four summaries.
Why is the median lower than the mean for the screen-time data?
practice.answer: A tail of high values pulls the mean upward; the median depends only on position.

practice.prompt: Group the screen data into 0–<60, 60–<120, 120–<180, 180–<240, 240–<300, 300–360 (last includes 360). Find frequencies.
practice.reasoning: Count each value once using the stated boundary rule.

practice.prompt: Why must a histogram state its interval boundaries?
practice.answer: A value on a boundary must belong to exactly one interval; otherwise counts can be duplicated or omitted.
practice.reasoning: Equal widths also make heights comparable.

practice.prompt: Estimate the mean from grouped intervals with midpoints 30, 90, 150, 210, 270, 330 and frequencies 1, 9, 9, 5, 3, 3.
practice.reasoning: Weighted midpoint sum ÷30 = 168. A grouped estimate need not equal the raw mean (158 minutes).

diagram.caption: Equal 60-minute intervals. Boundary rule: left endpoint included, right excluded; the final interval includes 360.

sections.title: Trends, comparisons and misleading graphs
sections.intent: Read the scale, denominator and time order before accepting a visual claim.
paras: A line graph or time-ordered bar chart can show change over time. Describe direction, size of change and exceptions; do not call every fluctuation a trend.
Misleading displays include truncated axes, unequal intervals, 3-D distortion, area used for a one-dimensional value, missing denominators and selective time windows. Compare like with like.

example.title: Test “sales doubled”
example.answer: The claim is false: sales rose by 80%, not 100%.

sections.warning: A percentage can be correct while the headline is misleading if the base is tiny or the denominator is hidden.

practice.prompt: Uptake over five years is 88, 72, 80, 90, 96. Describe the overall change and the largest fall.
practice.answer: Overall +8; largest fall 16 from year 1 to year 2.

practice.prompt: Find the percentage fall from 88 to 72.
A headline says “sales doubled” after 50 to 90. Test it.
A pictogram doubles both height and width for a value twice as large. Explain the distortion.
practice.answer: The area becomes four times as large, exaggerating a twofold value.
practice.reasoning: Area scales with the square of linear size.

practice.prompt: Year 9 off-site is 13/65; Year 7 is 8/70. Compare percentages fairly.
practice.reasoning: Use each year group as its denominator.

practice.prompt: Incidents rise from 2 to 4. Is “doubled” correct? What else should a reader ask?
practice.answer: Yes, 100% increase, but ask for the time period, population size and longer trend; small counts can make a dramatic headline.

diagram.caption: A zero-based axis shows the fall from 88 to 72 and the later recovery to 96 without exaggeration.

explore.title: How should data be grouped?
explore.instruction: Criterion B. Use the same 30 values with two interval widths, compare the pictures and justify a display for families.
explore.intro: Daily screen time (minutes), ordered: 45, 60, 60, 75, 80, 90, 90, 90, 105, 110, 120, 120, 120, 120, 135, 140, 150, 150, 165, 180, 180, 195, 210, 210, 240, 240, 270, 300, 330, 360. Boundary rule: left included, right excluded; final interval includes 360.

items.prompt: Find the six 60-minute frequencies.
items.reasoning: Count each value once.

items.prompt: Find the three 120-minute frequencies.
items.reasoning: Combine adjacent 60-minute intervals.

verify.expr: [sum(a<=x<(b if b<360 else 361) for x in SCREEN) for a,b in [(0,120),(120,240),(240,360)]]

items.prompt: Which grouping shows the central cluster more clearly? Which loses more detail?
items.answer: 60-minute intervals show the cluster around 60–180 more clearly; 120-minute intervals lose more detail.
items.reasoning: Narrower equal intervals preserve more shape.

items.prompt: Find mean, median, mode and range. How many students spend 240 minutes or more?
items.answer: Mean 158; median 137.5; mode 120; range 315 minutes. Six students are at 240 or more.
items.reasoning: Use the raw ordered data; count 240,240,270,300,330,360.

items.prompt: Test “the typical student spends four hours a day” and recommend a newsletter display.
items.answer: Not supported: mean 158 min, median 137.5 min; only 6/30=20% reach 240 min. Recommend a labelled 60-minute histogram with median and a note about the high-value tail.
items.reasoning: Choose an average and grouping that match the claim and audience.

application.title: The canteen survey
application.instruction: Criterion D. Simulated whole-school survey of 200 students. State denominators and distinguish spending from canteen revenue.
application.intro: Lunch choice by year group is shown below. Prices: school lunch $4.20, packed lunch ingredients about $3.10, off-site meal about $5.50. Five-year school-lunch uptake: 88, 72, 80, 90, 96.

items.prompt: Find the school-lunch percentage and the pie-chart angles for all three choices.
items.reasoning: Use denominator 200.

items.prompt: Compare off-site eating in Year 9 and Year 7 using percentages.
items.answer: Year 9: 20%; Year 7: about 11.4%.

items.prompt: Find daily spending by lunch choice and total spending. How much extra canteen revenue if 24 students switch from packed to school lunch?
items.answer: School $403.20; packed $229.40; off-site $165.00; total $797.60. Extra canteen revenue $100.80.
items.reasoning: Multiply counts by prices; the switch adds 24×4.20 to canteen revenue.

items.prompt: Evaluate “off-site eating is out of control” and write a more accurate headline of at most twelve words.
items.answer: Sample headline: “Off-site lunches are 15% overall, higher in Year 9.” The claim is not supported by one share alone; compare year groups and time data.
items.reasoning: 15% overall and 20% in Year 9 are descriptive, not proof of a crisis.

assessment.title: The data explainer
assessment.instruction: Criteria A and C. Choose a display, compute one summary and write a claim that the data actually support.
assessment.intro: Use the lunch survey to explain why a truncated bar chart or a single pie chart could mislead.

items.prompt: Which display best compares lunch choices across the three year groups? Explain.
items.answer: A clustered bar chart or two-way table; it preserves year-group comparisons.
items.reasoning: A single pie chart hides the year structure.

items.prompt: Calculate the school-lunch share and one check on the pie chart.
items.reasoning: The whole is 200 students.

items.prompt: Write one supported claim and one warning about a misleading display.
items.answer: Sample claim: “School lunch is the most common choice (48%).” Warning: a bar axis not starting at zero can exaggerate differences.
items.reasoning: The claim quotes a denominator and the warning names a visual distortion.

groups.title: Mixed practice 10
groups.instruction: Connect ideas. Give units and reasons where requested.

items.prompt: Classify “height in centimetres”.
items.answer: Continuous numerical.
items.reasoning: It is measured on a scale.

items.prompt: Find the sector angle for 74 out of 200.
Find mean, median, mode and range of 4, 4, 6, 10.
items.answer: Mean 6; median 5; mode 4; range 6.

items.prompt: A frequency table has counts 12, 18, 20. Find the percentage for 18.
Why can a truncated vertical axis mislead?
items.answer: It exaggerates visual differences by hiding the zero baseline.
items.reasoning: Bar height should be proportional to frequency.

items.prompt: Uptake falls from 90 to 72. Find the percentage fall.
A data set has mean 50 and median 30. What might explain the gap?
items.answer: A high-value tail or outliers pulling the mean upward.
items.reasoning: The median is resistant to extreme values.

items.prompt: Grouped intervals 0–<10 and 10–20 have frequencies 4 and 6. Estimate the mean using midpoints.
A survey of 80 has 20 choosing A. Find the percentage and pie angle.
A headline says “crime doubled” from 2 to 4 incidents. Give a balanced response.
items.answer: The 100% increase is correct, but the base is tiny; ask for population, time period and longer trend before judging risk.
items.reasoning: Relative change without context can mislead.
